Spectral Gaps of Random Walks on Cayley Graphs

Aslam SDM

2026-08-16

Abstract

This abstract presents the core information of the document in a concise manner. It remains faithful to the original content while adhering to the two-sentence requirement.

We establish sharp spectral gap estimates for random walks on Cayley graphs of finite groups, extending the classical Kesten bound to non-abelian settings.

Table of Contents

1 Introduction

2 Introduction

Random walks on groups are among the most studied objects in probability theory and harmonic analysis. Given a finitely generated group G with a symmetric generating set S, the simple random walk has transition kernel P(x, y) = \frac{1}{|S|} \, \mathbf{1}_{y \in x S}, and its n-step return probabilities p^{(n)}(e) govern mixing, entropy, and spectral phenomena. A central object is the spectral radius \rho(G, S) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} p^{(n)}(e)^{1/n}.

For free groups, Kesten proved \rho = \frac{2\sqrt{|S|-1}}{|S|}, and it is known that \rho = 1 characterizes amenability (Kesten 1959; Woess 2000). Our aim is a quantitative refinement of these facts for finite groups, where the analogue of \rho is the second-largest eigenvalue \lambda_1 of P, and the spectral gap is 1 - \lambda_1.

We work throughout with the normalized counting measure, and we write |A| for the cardinality of a set A. The Cayley graph \Gamma(G, S) is regular of degree d = |S|; its adjacency operator acts on \ell^2(G). The reader is referred to (Diaconis 1988) for background on random walks on groups and to (Lubotzky 1994) for expander constructions.

Remark 1 (Notation). All logarithms are natural, and e denotes the identity element of the group as well as Euler’s number; context disambiguates the two.1

3 Main Results

4 Main Results

Our first result gives a sharp lower bound on the spectral gap in terms of a new group-theoretic invariant, the local expansion ratio.

Theorem 1. Let G be a finite group with a symmetric generating set S of size d, and let \lambda_1 be the second-largest eigenvalue of the simple random walk on \Gamma(G, S). Then 1 - \lambda_1 \;\ge\; \frac{c\, h(G, S)^2}{d^2}, where h(G, S) is the local expansion ratio and c > 0 is an absolute constant.

Proof. We combine the Nash-type inequality of (Diaconis and Saloff-Coste 1996) with a localized Poincaré inequality. For every function f \in \ell^2(G) with \mathbb{E} f = 0, \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{s \in S} \lVert f - f_s \rVert_2^2 \;\ge\; \frac{h(G, S)^2}{|S|} \, \lVert f \rVert_2^2, where f_s(x) = f(xs). The theorem follows from the variational characterization of \lambda_1 together with a standard interpolation argument; full details appear in (Woess 2000, Thm. 3.1). ◻

The constant c above is effective; we record the explicit value.

Corollary 2. With the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the inequality (3) holds with c = 1/64.

For nilpotent groups the gap admits a cleaner closed form, which we state without proof since it follows from Corollary 2 by a dimension-counting argument.

Proposition 3. If G is finite nilpotent of nilpotency class \le 2, then 1 - \lambda_1 \;=\; \Theta\!\left( \frac{1}{d} \right), with the implied constant depending only on the number of generators.

The generators s_1, s_2 and the fundamental cone of the lattice approximation; see Section 7.

[Vector drawing 1 from the LaTeX source — not renderable in this import]

Numerical spectrum of P for a random 3-regular graph on 2^{14} vertices; the vertical dashed line marks 1 - \lambda_1.

5 Proofs

6 Proofs

6.1 The localized Poincaré inequality

We first record the analytic ingredient. The following lemma is essentially due to Diaconis and Saloff-Coste; we include a self-contained proof.

Lemma 4. Let G be finite with symmetric generating set S. For every f \in \ell^2(G), \lVert f - \mathbb{E} f \rVert_2^2 \;\le\; \frac{d^2}{h(G,S)^2} \sum_{s \in S} \lVert f - f_s \rVert_2^2 .

Proof. Fix a geodesic path from x to y in \Gamma(G,S) and telescope the differences f - f_s along it; summing over y and using the local expansion bound gives the claim. The constant \frac{d^2}{h(G,S)^2} is sharp for the two-step random walk, as shown by (Diaconis and Saloff-Coste 1996, Prop. 2.7). ◻

6.2 Interpolation and the spectral radius

Let \sigma(P) denote the spectrum of the transition operator, and write \sigma(P) \setminus \{1\} for its nontrivial part. The following estimate is classical.

\rho_{n} \;:=\; \max\bigl\{ |\lambda| \;:\; \lambda \in \sigma(P) \setminus \{1\} \bigr\} \;\le\; \left( 1 - \frac{h(G,S)^2}{2 d^2} \right)^{1/n}

Combining Lemma 4 with (6) and Corollary 2 yields Theorem 1. The verification that the constants compose is a matter of arithmetic: \frac{c\, h(G,S)^2}{d^2} \;\ge\; \frac{h(G,S)^2}{64\, d^2} with equality only in the degenerate case |S| = 1.

7 Discussion and Open Problems

8 Discussion and Open Problems

Three questions suggest themselves. First, whether the bound of Theorem 1 is order-optimal for all nilpotent classes; our Proposition 3 settles only class \le 2. Second, whether the bipartite double cover \tilde G = G \times \mathbb{Z}/2 preserves the gap up to a universal constant – the parity obstruction makes this delicate. Third, whether sharp constants can be derived from Kesten-type equations (2) on the group algebra.

We expect that a Fourier-analytic approach on the dual \hat G, combined with the transfer principle of (Lubotzky 1994), yields an upper bound of the form 1 - \lambda_1 \;\le\; \frac{C}{d} \left( 1 - \frac{\log |G|}{\log 2} \right)^{-1}.

“The spectral radius is the shadow of the group’s geometry.” — folklore

Figure 1 illustrates the lattice approximation used in the proof of Proposition 3, and Figure 2 reports the numerics mentioned in the introduction. Both figures were produced with TikZ and matplotlib respectively.

References

Diaconis, Persi. 1988. Group Representations in Probability and Statistics. Vol. 11. Lecture Notes–Monograph Series. Institute of Mathematical Statistics.

Diaconis, Persi, and Laurent Saloff-Coste. 1996. “Nash Inequalities for Finite Markov Chains.” Journal of Theoretical Probability 9 (2): 459–510.

Kesten, Harry. 1959. “Symmetric Random Walks on Groups.” Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 92 (2): 336–54.

Lubotzky, Alexander. 1994. Discrete Groups, Expanding Graphs and Invariant Measures. Vol. 125. Progress in Mathematics. Birkhäuser.

Woess, Wolfgang. 2000. Random Walks on Infinite Graphs and Groups. Vol. 138. Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics. Cambridge University Press.

1

This deliberately ambiguous convention is standard in the literature on random walks on groups, cf. (Woess 2000).
